Statistic measuring inter-rater agreement for categorical items [...] Kappa is an index that considers observed agreement with respect to a baseline agreement. However, investigators must consider carefully whether Kappa's baseline agreement is relevant for the particular research question. Kappa's baseline is frequently described as the agreement due to chance, which is only partially correct. Kappa's baseline agreement is the agreement that would be expected due to random allocation, given the quantities specified by the marginal totals of square contingency table. Thus, κ = 0 when the observed allocation is apparently random, regardless of the quantity disagreement as constrained by the marginal totals. However, for many applications, investigators should be more interested in the quantity disagreement in the marginal totals than in the allocation

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Statistical measure of inter-rater agreement

**Krippendorff's alpha coefficient**,[[1]](#cite_note-1) named after academic [Klaus Krippendorff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Klaus_Krippendorff "Klaus Krippendorff"), is a statistical measure of the agreement achieved when coding a set of units of analysis. Since the 1970s, *alpha* has been used in [content analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Content_analysis "Content analysis") where textual units are categorized by trained readers, in counseling and [survey research](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Survey_research "Survey research") where experts code open-ended interview data into analyzable terms, in [psychological testing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychological_testing "Psychological testing") where alternative tests of the same phenomena need to be compared, or in [observational studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Observational_studies "Observational studies") where unstructured happenings are recorded for subsequent analysis.

Krippendorff's alpha generalizes several known statistics, often called measures of inter-coder agreement, [inter-rater reliability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inter-rater_reliability "Inter-rater reliability"), reliability of coding given sets of units (as distinct from unitizing) but it also distinguishes itself from statistics that are called reliability coefficients but are unsuitable to the particulars of coding data generated for subsequent analysis.

Krippendorff's alpha is applicable to any number of coders, each assigning one value to one unit of analysis, to incomplete (missing) data, to any number of values available for coding a variable, to binary, nominal, ordinal, interval, ratio, polar, and circular metrics (note that this is not a metric in the mathematical sense, but often the square of a [mathematical metric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distance#Mathematical_formalization "Distance"), see [levels of measurement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levels_of_measurement "Levels of measurement")), and it adjusts itself to small sample sizes of the reliability data. The virtue of a single coefficient with these variations is that computed reliabilities are comparable across any numbers of coders, values, different metrics, and unequal sample sizes.

Software for calculating Krippendorff's alpha is available.[[2]](#cite_note-2)[[3]](#cite_note-3)[[4]](#cite_note-4)[[5]](#cite_note-5)[[6]](#cite_note-6)[[7]](#cite_note-7)[[8]](#cite_note-8)[[9]](#cite_note-9)

## Reliability data

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Krippendorff%27s_alpha&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Reliability data")]

Reliability data are generated in a situation in which *m* ≥ 2 jointly instructed (e.g., by a [code book](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Code_book "Code book")) but independently working coders assign any one of a set of values 1,...,*V* to a common set of *N* units of analysis. In their canonical form, reliability data are tabulated in an *m*-by-*N* matrix containing *N* values *vij* that coder *ci* has assigned to unit *uj*. Define *mj* as the number of values assigned to unit *j* across all coders *c*. When data are incomplete, *mj* may be less than *m*. Reliability data require that values be pairable, i.e., *mj* ≥ 2. The total number of pairable values is ![{\displaystyle \sum _{j=1}^{N}m_{j}=}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/1b9f8cf7a67c915c59a32c707de8fcea01a2a0c6) *n* ≤ *mN*.

To help clarify, here is what the canonical form looks like, in the abstract:

|  | *u*1 | *u*2 | *u*3 | ... | *uN* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| *c*1 | *v*11 | *v*12 | *v*13 | ⋯ | *v*1*N* |
| *c*2 | *v*21 | *v*22 | *v*23 | ⋯ | *v*2*N* |
| *c*3 | *v*31 | *v*32 | *v*33 | ⋯ | *v*3*N* |
| ⋮ | ⋮ | ⋮ | ⋮ | ⋱ | ⋮ |
| *c**m* | *v**m*1 | *v**m*2 | *v**m*3 | ⋯ | *v**mN* |

## General form of alpha

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Krippendorff%27s_alpha&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: General form of alpha")]

We denote by ![{\displaystyle R}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/4b0bfb3769bf24d80e15374dc37b0441e2616e33) the set of all possible responses an observer can give. The responses of all observers for an example is called a unit (it forms a multiset). We denote a multiset with these units as the items, ![{\displaystyle U}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/458a728f53b9a0274f059cd695e067c430956025).

Alpha is given by:

:   ![{\displaystyle \alpha =1-{\frac {D_{o}}{D_{e}}}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/cfd662db66cc0883d4d6e2f7729e02b5173059e7)

where ![{\displaystyle D_{o}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/91badd96610c65259154624aaa20a1375c7b8015) is the disagreement observed and ![{\displaystyle D_{e}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/37e785a9fc0aea966a290a076cd916bff798900a) is the disagreement expected by chance.

:   ![{\displaystyle D_{o}={\frac {1}{n}}\sum _{c\in R}\sum _{k\in R}\delta (c,k)\sum _{u\in U}m_{u}{\frac {n_{cku}}{P(m_{u},2)}}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/dd397a489bf019f6b4bf37d1646d134207332bb6)

where ![{\displaystyle \delta }](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/c5321cfa797202b3e1f8620663ff43c4660ea03a) is a metric function (note that this is not a metric in the mathematical sense, but often the square of a mathematical metric, see below), ![{\displaystyle n}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/a601995d55609f2d9f5e233e36fbe9ea26011b3b) is the total number of pairable elements, ![{\displaystyle m_{u}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/c24c968c4ba7b6d62941075cdfddee7d3aa574bb) is the number of items in a unit, ![{\displaystyle n_{cku}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/219749ae45d87950aa46a850549bc64223cd8595) number of ![{\displaystyle (c,k)}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/134a0e3a0c2d472a113eb4994d2c5d022abddfd5) pairs in unit ![{\displaystyle u}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/c3e6bb763d22c20916ed4f0bb6bd49d7470cffd8), and ![{\displaystyle P}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/b4dc73bf40314945ff376bd363916a738548d40a) is the [permutation function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Permutation#k-permutations_of_n "Permutation"). Rearranging terms, the sum can be interpreted in a conceptual way as the weighted average of the disagreements of the individual units weighted by the number of coders assigned to unit j:

![{\displaystyle D_{o}={\frac {1}{n}}\sum _{j=1}^{N}m_{j}\,\mathbb {E} (\delta _{j})}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/d0c74358871c57368dd780cae6f67d597bdd8fbd)

where ![{\displaystyle \mathbb {E} (\delta _{j})}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/4f4a35498ea5cc04f921c5add8c31a33f60dcae0) is the mean of the ![{\displaystyle m_{j} \choose 2}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/9fac14f19b71e286e4d7fabd4f263be6068f89c9) numbers ![{\displaystyle \delta (v_{ij},v_{i'j})}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/756a731867fc7f9a56ceb5bbb200904e33ecdaff) (here ![{\displaystyle i>i'}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/d64c3b383e20e29462555eaed7b4500f9486c1af) and define pairable elements). Note that in the case ![{\displaystyle m_{j}=m}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/4125f67f59e0e1d6de3e8e6355574ac3003e4951) for all ![{\displaystyle j}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/2f461e54f5c093e92a55547b9764291390f0b5d0), ![{\displaystyle D_{o}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/91badd96610c65259154624aaa20a1375c7b8015) is just the average all the numbers ![{\displaystyle \delta (v_{ij},v_{i'j})}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/756a731867fc7f9a56ceb5bbb200904e33ecdaff) with ![{\displaystyle i>i'}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/d64c3b383e20e29462555eaed7b4500f9486c1af). From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Statistical measure

**Fleiss's kappa** is a [statistical measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistical_measure "Statistical measure") for assessing the [reliability of agreement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inter-rater_reliability "Inter-rater reliability") between a fixed number of [raters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rater "Rater") when assigning [categorical ratings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Categorical_rating "Categorical rating") to a number of items. This contrasts with other kappas such as [Cohen's kappa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cohen's_kappa "Cohen's kappa"), which only work when assessing the agreement between two raters or the intra-rater reliability (for one appraiser versus themself). The measure calculates the degree of agreement in classification beyond what would be expected by chance. It is named after American biostatistician [Joseph L. Fleiss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_L._Fleiss "Joseph L. Fleiss"), who introduced it in a 1971 article.[[1]](#cite_note-Fleiss1971-1)

Fleiss's kappa can be used with binary or [nominal-scale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nominal_data "Nominal data"). It can also be applied to [ordinal data](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordinal_data "Ordinal data") (ranked data): the MiniTab online documentation gives an example.[[2]](#cite_note-MiniTab-2) However, this document notes: "When you have ordinal ratings, such as defect severity ratings on a scale of 1–5, [Kendall's coefficients](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kendall_rank_correlation_coefficient "Kendall rank correlation coefficient"), which account for ordering, are usually more appropriate statistics to determine association than kappa alone." Keep in mind that Kendall's rank coefficients are only appropriate for rank data.

## Introduction

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Fleiss%27s_kappa&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Introduction")]

Fleiss's kappa is a generalisation of [Scott's pi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott's_pi "Scott's pi") statistic, a [statistical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistical "Statistical") measure of [inter-rater reliability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inter-rater_reliability "Inter-rater reliability").[[3]](#cite_note-Scott1955-3) It is also related to Cohen's kappa statistic and [Youden's J statistic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Youden's_J_statistic "Youden's J statistic"), which may be more appropriate in certain instances.[[4]](#cite_note-Powers2012-4) Whereas Scott's pi and Cohen's kappa work for only two raters, Fleiss's kappa works for any number of raters, giving categorical ratings, to a fixed number of items, under the condition that for each item, raters are randomly sampled. It can be interpreted as the extent to which the observed agreement among raters exceeds what would be expected if all raters made their ratings completely at random. Whereas Cohen's kappa assumes the same two raters have rated a set of items, Fleiss's kappa specifically allows that although there are a fixed number of raters (e.g., three), different items may be rated by different individuals.[[1]](#cite_note-Fleiss1971-1) That is, Item 1 is rated by Raters A, B, and C; but Item 2 could be rated by Raters D, E, and F. The condition of random sampling among raters makes Fleiss's kappa not suited for cases where all raters rate all patients.[[5]](#cite_note-Hallgren2012-5)

Agreement can be thought of as follows: If a fixed number of people assign numerical ratings to a number of items, then the kappa will give a measure of how consistent the ratings are. The kappa ![{\displaystyle \kappa }](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/54ddec2e922c5caea4e47d04feef86e782dc8e6d) can be defined as,[[5]](#cite_note-Hallgren2012-5) ![{\displaystyle \kappa ={\frac {{\bar {P}}-{\bar {P_{e}}}}{1-{\bar {P_{e}}}}}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/3ddcff10b2722907e317bf0a0eaa360af3ef3303)

The factor ![{\displaystyle 1-{\bar {P_{e}}}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/54e0516141a1624c5c8a94a925363c28a116a312) gives the degree of agreement that is attainable above chance, and ![{\displaystyle {\bar {P}}-{\bar {P_{e}}}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/50220ed3a108b0bcdcba0721ebfa36baf7d0f81f) gives the degree of agreement achieved above chance. If the raters are in complete agreement, then ![{\displaystyle \kappa =1~}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/ee17cef0be4931b4acdf19e1f4088edf267a1e6f). If there is no agreement among the raters (other than what would be expected by chance), then ![{\displaystyle \kappa \leq 0}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/7d42692898de230f7b1fdd8f4ac5b51562591201).[[5]](#cite_note-Hallgren2012-5)

Conger's kappa is more robust than Fleiss's kappa (it corrects for chance occurrences), but requires that all items be rated by all the raters [[6]](#cite_note-6).

## Definition

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Fleiss%27s_kappa&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Definition")]

|  |
| --- |
| This section **does not [cite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing_sources "Wikipedia:Citing sources") any [sources](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability "Wikipedia:Verifiability")**. Please help [improve this section](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:EditPage/Fleiss's_kappa "Special:EditPage/Fleiss's kappa") by [adding citations to reliable sources](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Referencing_for_beginners "Help:Referencing for beginners"). Unsourced material may be challenged and [removed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Burden_of_evidence "Wikipedia:Verifiability"). *(November 2025)* *([Learn how and when to remove this message](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Maintenance_template_removal "Help:Maintenance template removal"))* |

Let N be the total number of elements, let n be the number of ratings per element, and let k be the number of categories into which assignments are made. The elements are indexed by *i* = 1, ..., *N* and the categories are indexed by *j* = 1, ..., *k*. Let *n**ij* represent the number of raters who assigned the i-th element to the j-th category.[[1]](#cite_note-Fleiss1971-1)

First calculate *p**j*, the proportion of all assignments which were to the j-th category: ![{\displaystyle p_{j}={\frac {1}{Nn}}\sum _{i=1}^{N}n_{ij},\quad \quad 1=\sum _{j=1}^{k}p_{j}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/fe956c121122233aaaa56f3bf15bd746dd2f0ecb) Now calculate ![{\displaystyle P_{i}\,}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/539193d3e3af20578edb578d587218ca8b096df4), the extent to which raters agree for the i-th element (i.e., compute how many rater-rater pairs are in agreement, relative to the number of all possible rater-rater pairs): ![{\displaystyle {\begin{aligned}P_{i}&={\frac {1}{n(n-1)}}\sum _{j=1}^{k}n_{ij}(n_{ij}-1)\\&={\frac {1}{n(n-1)}}\sum _{j=1}^{k}(n_{ij}^{2}-n_{ij})\\&={\frac {1}{n(n-1)}}{\biggl [}\sum _{j=1}^{k}{\bigl (}n_{ij}^{2}{\bigr )}-n{\biggr ]}\end{aligned}}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/c0c16d7bdb5c222b25881d3cd075759264bc7829) Note that ![{\displaystyle P_{i}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/3ba1396129f7be3c7f828a571b6649e6807d10d3) is bound between 0, when ratings are assigned equally over all categories, and 1, when all ratings are assigned to a single category.

Now compute ![{\displaystyle {\bar {P}}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/f9d1fdaf8f50ca1bfe522c83b892dd55f87659fe), the mean of the ![{\displaystyle P_{i}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/3ba1396129f7be3c7f828a571b6649e6807d10d3)'s, and ![{\displaystyle {\bar {P_{e}}}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/dbdd2c966bf7b50a504386981b8d262b575a25b1), which go into the formula for ![{\displaystyle \kappa }](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/54ddec2e922c5caea4e47d04feef86e782dc8e6d): ![{\displaystyle {\begin{aligned}{\bar {P}}&={\frac {1}{N}}\sum _{i=1}^{N}P_{i}={\frac {1}{Nn(n-1)}}{\biggl [}\sum _{i=1}^{N}\sum _{j=1}^{k}{\bigl (}n_{ij}^{2}{\bigr )}-Nn{\biggr ]}\\{\bar {P_{e}}}&=\sum _{j=1}^{k}p_{j}^{2}\end{aligned}}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/d085d6229097a8382e47cdfbe3346bf6ff1c1744)

Kappa statistics such as Fleiss' kappa and Cohen's kappa are methods for calculating inter-rater reliability based on different assumptions about the marginal or prior distributions, and are increasingly used as chance corrected alternatives to accuracy in other contexts (including the multiclass case). From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Index that describes the performance of a dichotomous diagnostic test

**Youden's J statistic** (also called **Youden's index**) is a single statistic that captures the performance of a [dichotomous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dichotomy "Dichotomy") diagnostic test. In [meteorology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meteorology "Meteorology"), this statistic is referred to as **Peirce Skill Score (PSS)**, **Hanssen–Kuipers Discriminant (HKD)**, or **True Skill Statistic (TSS)**.[[1]](#cite_note-1)

## Definition

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Youden%27s_J_statistic&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Definition")]

Youden's *J* statistic is

:   ![{\displaystyle J={\text{sensitivity}}+{\text{specificity}}-1={\text{recall}}_{1}+{\text{recall}}_{0}-1=TPR+TNR-1}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/00e1410754f4478a6ddb8be5a00e6657a926ae2a)

with the two right-hand quantities being [sensitivity and specificity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sensitivity_and_specificity "Sensitivity and specificity"). Thus the expanded formula is:

:   ![{\displaystyle J={\frac {\mathit {TP}}{{\mathit {TP}}+{\mathit {FN}}}}+{\frac {\mathit {TN}}{{\mathit {TN}}+{\mathit {FP}}}}-1={\frac {{\mathit {TP}}\times {\mathit {TN}}-{\mathit {FP}}\times {\mathit {FN}}}{({\mathit {TP}}+{\mathit {FN}})({\mathit {TN}}+{\mathit {FP}})}}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/27b8957168f8d72ae82f89099eec67940cfd4f04)

In this equation, TP is the number of true positives, TN the number of true negatives, FP the number of false positives and FN the number of false negatives.

The index was suggested by [W. J. Youden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_J._Youden "William J. Youden") in 1950[[2]](#cite_note-Youden1950-2) as a way of summarising the performance of a diagnostic test; however, the formula was earlier published in *Science* by [C. S. Peirce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Sanders_Peirce "Charles Sanders Peirce") in 1884.[[3]](#cite_note-3) Its value ranges from -1 through 1 (inclusive),[[2]](#cite_note-Youden1950-2) and has a zero value when a diagnostic test gives the same proportion of positive results for groups with and without the disease, i.e the test is useless. A value of 1 indicates that there are no false positives or false negatives, i.e. the test is perfect. The index gives equal weight to false positive and false negative values, so all tests with the same value of the index give the same proportion of total misclassified results. While it is possible to obtain a value of less than zero from this equation, e.g. Classification yields only False Positives and False Negatives, a value of less than zero just indicates that the positive and negative labels have been switched. After correcting the labels the result will then be in the 0 through 1 range.

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1b/ROC_Curve_T1D_Validation%2C_top5_r2filtered.svg/250px-ROC_Curve_T1D_Validation%2C_top5_r2filtered.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:ROC_Curve_T1D_Validation,_top5_r2filtered.svg)

Example of a receiver operating characteristic curve.

ROC curve

Chance level

J: maximum value of Youden's index for the ROC curve

Youden's index is often used in conjunction with [receiver operating characteristic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Receiver_operating_characteristic "Receiver operating characteristic") (ROC) analysis.[[4]](#cite_note-Schisterman2005-4) The index is defined for all points of an ROC curve, and the maximum value of the index may be used as a criterion for selecting the optimum cut-off point when a diagnostic test gives a numeric rather than a dichotomous result. The index is represented graphically as the height above the chance line, and it is also equivalent to the area under the curve subtended by a single operating point.[[5]](#cite_note-Powers2007-5) Because the ROC curve almost always forms a convex curve, the line of this maximum index value is likely to intersect the ROC curve at the point where the ROC curve is closest to the point in the top left corner (i.e. the point closest to no false positive or false negative results).

## Confidence interval

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Youden%27s_J_statistic&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Confidence interval")]

For a given diagnostic test with ![{\displaystyle n_{\text{sensitivity}}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/2d34166d283fbe5e53db41a0edcb1341a87c916a) diseased subjects and ![{\displaystyle n_{\text{specificity}}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/2d35131273882f93011d13fa226e11a81fef1cbb) healthy subjects, the Youden Index can be equivalently expressed as the difference between the [true positive rate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sensitivity_and_specificity "Sensitivity and specificity") (sensitivity) and the [false positive rate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/False_positive_rate "False positive rate") (1 − specificity):

:   ![{\displaystyle {\hat {J}}={\hat {p}}_{\text{sensitivity}}-{\hat {p}}_{\text{FPR}}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/77b5886ae6598fb297bbe7cb319e51f24042e709)

where ![{\displaystyle {\hat {p}}_{\text{FPR}}=1-{\hat {p}}_{\text{specificity}}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/24734f2193fcb7b41ddbf1bddaab7d837f88afff). Written this way, *J* is a difference of two independent binomial proportions estimated from the diseased and healthy subgroups. Inference for *J* (with a fixed, pre-specified threshold) therefore reduces directly to inference for the difference of two proportions, and the standard machinery of the [two-proportion *Z*-test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-proportion_Z-test "Two-proportion Z-test") applies.[[6]](#cite_note-Shan2015-6)

In particular, the [Wald (1 − α) confidence interval for the difference of two proportions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-proportion_Z-test#Confidence_interval "Two-proportion Z-test") gives:

:   ![{\displaystyle CI={\hat {J}}\pm z_{1-\alpha /2}{\sqrt {{\frac {{\hat {p}}_{\text{sensitivity}}(1-{\hat {p}}_{\text{sensitivity}})}{n_{\text{sensitivity}}}}+{\frac {{\hat {p}}_{\text{FPR}}(1-{\hat {p}}_{\text{FPR}})}{n_{\text{FPR}}}}}}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/09f6dd2b10184f045ca26f8bc38ac43a0ddc3388)

where ![{\displaystyle z_{1-\alpha /2}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/c01063bb39409347638136f9dd229daab24f81cf) is the critical value from the standard [normal distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normal_distribution "Normal distribution") (e.g., 1.96 for a 95% confidence interval). Since the false positive rate and the specificity are estimated from the same healthy subgroup, ![{\displaystyle n_{\text{FPR}}=n_{\text{specificity}}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/268d047d1b9c8f86adb3cb41638716590dd472a0), and the variance contribution from that subgroup is identical whether parameterized by FPR or specificity:

:   ![{\displaystyle {\frac {{\hat {p}}_{\text{FPR}}(1-{\hat {p}}_{\text{FPR}})}{n_{\text{FPR}}}}={\frac {(1-{\hat {p}}_{\text{specificity}})\,{\hat {p}}_{\text{specificity}}}{n_{\text{specificity}}}}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/574038a9c0d4b11df2f6adf352454fb9b252c8de)

So this CI is equivalent to the classical Wald interval expressed in terms of sensitivity and specificity.

If the threshold is instead optimized to maximize *J*, the variance estimate must account for the additional variability of the threshold selection process. In such cases, the [Delta method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delta_method "Delta method") or [bootstrapping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bootstrapping_(statistics) "Bootstrapping (statistics)") is required to maintain the nominal coverage probability.[[7]](#cite_note-Schisterman2007b-7)[[8]](#cite_note-Fluss2005-8)

### Alternative estimation methods

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Youden%27s_J_statistic&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Alternative estimation methods")]

While the Wald interval is widely utilized, it may exhibit poor coverage probabilities or produce bounds outside the logical range of [−1, 1] when sample sizes are small or when proportions are near 0 or 1. Because *J* is a difference of two independent proportions, any confidence-interval method developed for the [two-proportion *Z*-test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-proportion_Z-test "Two-proportion Z-test") can be applied directly. Type of statistical analysis

**Nonparametric statistics** is a type of statistical analysis that makes minimal assumptions about the underlying [distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distribution_(mathematics) "Distribution (mathematics)") of the data being studied. Often these models are infinite-dimensional, rather than finite dimensional, as in [parametric statistics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parametric_statistics "Parametric statistics").[[1]](#cite_note-1) Nonparametric statistics can be used for [descriptive statistics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Descriptive_statistics "Descriptive statistics") or [statistical inference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistical_inference "Statistical inference"). Nonparametric tests are often used when the assumptions of parametric tests are evidently violated.[[2]](#cite_note-2)

## Definitions

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Nonparametric_statistics&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Definitions")]

The term "nonparametric statistics" has been defined imprecisely in the following two ways, among others:

The first meaning of *nonparametric* involves techniques that do not rely on data belonging to any particular parametric family of probability distributions. These include, among others:

* Methods which are *distribution-free*, which do not rely on assumptions that the data are drawn from a given parametric family of [probability distributions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probability_distributions "Probability distributions").
* Statistics defined to be a function on a sample, without dependency on a [parameter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parameter "Parameter").

An example is [order statistics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_statistic "Order statistic"), which are based on [ordinal ranking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ranking#Ordinal_ranking_( "Ranking") of observations.

The discussion following is taken from *Kendall's Advanced Theory of Statistics*.[[3]](#cite_note-3)

> Statistical hypotheses concern the behavior of observable random variables... For example, the hypothesis (a) that a normal distribution has a specified mean and variance is statistical; so is the hypothesis (b) that it has a given mean but unspecified variance; so is the hypothesis (c) that a distribution is of normal form with both mean and variance unspecified; finally, so is the hypothesis (d) that two unspecified continuous distributions are identical.
>
> It will have been noticed that in the examples (a) and (b) the distribution underlying the observations was taken to be of a certain form (the normal) and the hypothesis was concerned entirely with the value of one or both of its parameters. Such a hypothesis, for obvious reasons, is called *parametric*.
>
> Hypothesis (c) was of a different nature, as no parameter values are specified in the statement of the hypothesis; we might reasonably call such a hypothesis *nonparametric*. Hypothesis (d) is also nonparametric but, in addition, it does not even specify the underlying form of the distribution and may now be reasonably termed *distribution-free*. Notwithstanding these distinctions, the statistical literature now commonly applies the label "nonparametric" to test procedures that we have just termed "distribution-free", thereby losing a useful classification.

The second meaning of *nonparametric* involves techniques that do not assume that the *structure* of a model is fixed. Typically, the model grows in size to accommodate the complexity of the data. In these techniques, individual variables *are* typically assumed to belong to parametric distributions, and assumptions about the types of associations among variables are also made. These techniques include, among others:

* *[nonparametric regression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonparametric_regression "Nonparametric regression")*, which is modeling whereby the structure of the relationship between variables is treated nonparametrically, but where nevertheless there may be parametric assumptions about the distribution of model residuals.
* *nonparametric hierarchical Bayesian models*, such as models based on the [Dirichlet process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet_process "Dirichlet process"), which allow the number of [latent variables](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latent_variables "Latent variables") to grow as necessary to fit the data, but where individual variables still follow parametric distributions and even the process controlling the rate of growth of latent variables follows a parametric distribution.

## Applications and purpose

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Nonparametric_statistics&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Applications and purpose")]

Nonparametric methods are widely used for studying populations that have a ranked order (such as movie reviews receiving one to five "stars"). The use of nonparametric methods may be necessary when data have a [ranking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ranking "Ranking") but no clear [numerical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Number "Number") interpretation, such as when assessing [preferences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preferences "Preferences"). In terms of [levels of measurement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Level_of_measurement "Level of measurement"), nonparametric methods result in [ordinal data](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordinal_data "Ordinal data").

**Jacob Cohen** (April 20, 1923 – January 20, 1998)[[3]](#cite_note-jama-3) was an American [psychologist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychologist "Psychologist") and [statistician](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistician "Statistician") best known for his work on [statistical power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistical_power "Statistical power") and [effect size](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Effect_size "Effect size"), which helped to lay foundations for current statistical [meta-analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meta-analysis "Meta-analysis")[[4]](#cite_note-Saxon-4)[[5]](#cite_note-5)[[3]](#cite_note-jama-3) and the methods of [estimation statistics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estimation_statistics "Estimation statistics"). He gave his name to such measures as [Cohen's kappa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cohen's_kappa "Cohen's kappa"), [Cohen's *d*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cohen's_d "Cohen's d"), and [Cohen's *h*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cohen's_h "Cohen's h").[[6]](#cite_note-6)[[7]](#cite_note-7)

## Education and career

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Jacob_Cohen_(statistician)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Education and career")]

Cohen grew up in a Yiddish-speaking household and learned English at school. He attended the [Townsend Harris High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Townsend_Harris_High_School "Townsend Harris High School") and graduated at the age of 15. He entered the [City College of New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_College_of_New_York "City College of New York"), where he first studied mathematics but was interrupted by a service in the [US Army intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Army_intelligence "US Army intelligence") during [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") in Europe.[[1]](#cite_note-ampsych-1) He eventually received a BA in psychology in 1947 from the City College.[[4]](#cite_note-Saxon-4) He then obtained his Master's degree in 1948 and PhD in clinical psychology at [New York University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_University "New York University") (NYU) in 1950. His PhD advisor was Avrum Ben-Avi.[[2]](#cite_note-thesis-2) Cohen worked in the hospitals affiliated with the [Veterans Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Veterans_Administration "Veterans Administration") after graduation, first at Bronx, then at Montrose VA Medical Center, where he was a director of research.[[1]](#cite_note-ampsych-1) Between 1959 and retirement in 1993, he worked in the psychology department at NYU, latterly as the head of the [quantitative psychology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantitative_psychology "Quantitative psychology") group.[[4]](#cite_note-Saxon-4) In 1969 Cohen married Patricia Ruth Childs (1936-2018), later Patricia Cohen, who was a former PhD student in psychology at NYU.[[8]](#cite_note-8)

After retirement from NYU, Cohen continued working as a statistical consultant at the [Columbia Presbyterian Medical Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Presbyterian_Medical_Center "Columbia Presbyterian Medical Center"), [New York State Psychiatric Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_State_Psychiatric_Institute "New York State Psychiatric Institute"), and at their joint H.I.V. Center for Clinical and Behavioral Studies. Cohen passed away in 1998 at the [St. Vincent's Hospital and Medical Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Vincent's_Hospital_and_Medical_Center "St. Vincent's Hospital and Medical Center") in New York City.[[4]](#cite_note-Saxon-4)

Cohen was president of the [Society of Multivariate Experimental Psychology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Society_of_Multivariate_Experimental_Psychology "Society of Multivariate Experimental Psychology") in 1969. He was awarded the Distinguished Lifetime Achievement Award by the [American Psychological Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Psychological_Association "American Psychological Association") in 1997 and was a fellow of the [American Association for the Advancement of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Association_for_the_Advancement_of_Science "American Association for the Advancement of Science"), the American Psychological Association and the [American Statistical Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Statistical_Association "American Statistical Association").[[4]](#cite_note-Saxon-4)

## Power analysis and significance testing

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Jacob_Cohen_(statistician)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Power analysis and significance testing")]

In addition to being an advocate of power analysis and effect size, Cohen was a critic of reliance on, and lack of understanding of, [significance testing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Significance_testing "Significance testing") procedures used in statistics, especially misunderstandings of [null hypothesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Null_hypothesis "Null hypothesis") significance testing.[[9]](#cite_note-9) In particular, he identified the "near universal misinterpretation of p as the probability that H0 is false, the misinterpretation that its complement is the probability of successful replication, and the mistaken assumption that if one rejects H0 one thereby affirms the theory that led to the test".[[10]](#cite_note-10) He encouraged instead a recognition of single studies as exploratory and a reliance on [replication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Replication_(statistics) "Replication (statistics)") for support. Cohen developed known interpretation thresholds for the correlation *r* and the standardized mean difference *d*.[[11]](#cite_note-11)

Statistical measure of association for two binary variables

In [statistics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics "Statistics"), the **phi coefficient**, also known as the **mean square contingency coefficient** or **Yule coefficient of correlation** and commonly denoted by *φ* or *r**φ*, is a measure of [association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Correlation "Correlation") between two [binary variables](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_variables "Binary variables"). In [machine learning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machine_learning "Machine learning") and [bioinformatics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bioinformatics "Bioinformatics"), it is known as the **Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC)**. In [meteorology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meteorology "Meteorology") and elsewhere, it is referred to as the **Doolittle Measure of Association** or **Doolittle Skill Score**. Described by [Udny Yule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Udny_Yule "Udny Yule") in 1912[[1]](#cite_note-Yule_1912_579–652-1) and given the name *phi* by [Karl Pearson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Pearson "Karl Pearson") in the 1930s,[[2]](#cite_note-Cramer,_H._1946_p._282-2) it is a [special case](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_case "Special case") of the [Pearson correlation coefficient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pearson_correlation_coefficient "Pearson correlation coefficient").

## Definition

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Phi_coefficient&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Definition")]

A [Pearson correlation coefficient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pearson_correlation_coefficient "Pearson correlation coefficient") estimated for two binary variables will return the phi coefficient.[[3]](#cite_note-3)

Two binary variables are considered positively associated if most of the data falls along the diagonal cells. In contrast, two binary variables are considered negatively associated if most of the data falls off the diagonal.

If we have a 2×2 table for two random variables *x* and *y*

|  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *y* = 1 | *y* = 0 | total |
| *x* = 1 | {\displaystyle n_{11}} | {\displaystyle n_{10}} | {\displaystyle n_{1\bullet }} |
| *x* = 0 | {\displaystyle n_{01}} | {\displaystyle n_{00}} | {\displaystyle n_{0\bullet }} |
| total | {\displaystyle n_{\bullet 1}} | {\displaystyle n_{\bullet 0}} | {\displaystyle n} |

where *n*11, *n*10, *n*01, *n*00, are non-negative counts of numbers of observations that sum to *n*, the total number of observations. The phi coefficient that describes the association of *x* and *y* is

:   ![{\displaystyle \varphi ={\frac {n_{11}n_{00}-n_{10}n_{01}}{\sqrt {n_{1\bullet }n_{0\bullet }n_{\bullet 0}n_{\bullet 1}}}}.}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/9ed5b20c055bcc46e33d1b523bee3aaa9064706b)

Phi is related to the [point-biserial correlation coefficient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point-biserial_correlation_coefficient "Point-biserial correlation coefficient") and Cohen's *d* and estimates the extent of the relationship between two variables (2×2).[[4]](#cite_note-Ref_-4)

The phi coefficient can also be expressed using only ![{\displaystyle n}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/a601995d55609f2d9f5e233e36fbe9ea26011b3b), ![{\displaystyle n_{11}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/c1376673d425f46c3ce5383c4944108c7941e2cf), ![{\displaystyle n_{1\bullet }}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/cb2946a6c46cc71da3d9087306fa1d8d6ba119d6), and ![{\displaystyle n_{\bullet 1}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/1aceb26fc8338e71b942fbf8ee8f60f13bcc7f6b), as

:   ![{\displaystyle \varphi ={\frac {nn_{11}-n_{1\bullet }n_{\bullet 1}}{\sqrt {n_{1\bullet }n_{\bullet 1}(n-n_{1\bullet })(n-n_{\bullet 1})}}}.}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/e68f652be0818201e8069144d05ad25a8dcadbfa)

## Maximum values

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Phi_coefficient&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Maximum values")]

In general, the Pearson correlation coefficient ranges from −1 to +1, where ±1 indicates perfect agreement or disagreement, and 0 indicates no relationship. The range of the phi coefficient—a special case of the Pearson correlation coefficient—is more tightly bound when either of the binary variables are class-imbalanced.[[5]](#cite_note-5)

## Meteorology

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Phi_coefficient&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Meteorology")]

In [meteorology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meteorology "Meteorology"), the phi coefficient is referred to as the Doolittle Skill Score or the Doolittle Measure of Association,[[6]](#cite_note-6) though this is actually off by a square root: Doolittle's original 1885 statistic matches phi squared, not phi itself.[[7]](#cite_note-7) It was used by M. H. Doolittle in the 1880s to rate the accuracy of [meteorologist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meteorologist "Meteorologist") [John Park Finley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Park_Finley "John Park Finley")'s [tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado "Tornado") predictions and other [weather forecasts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_forecasts "Weather forecasts").

## Machine learning

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Phi_coefficient&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Machine learning")]

The Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) is widely used in the fields of bioinformatics and machine learning to evaluate the quality of binary (two-class) [classifications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_classification "Binary classification"). It is named for biochemist [Brian W. Matthews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Matthews_(biochemist) "Brian Matthews (biochemist)"), who described the measure in a foundational 1975 paper.[[8]](#cite_note-Matthews1975-8)

The coefficient accounts for true and false positives and negatives and is generally regarded as a balanced measure which can be used even if the classes are of very different sizes.[[9]](#cite_note-Boughorbel2017-9) The MCC is in essence a correlation coefficient between the observed and predicted binary classifications; it returns a value between −1 and +1. A coefficient of +1 represents a perfect prediction, 0 no better than random prediction and −1 indicates total disagreement between prediction and observation. However, if MCC equals neither −1, 0, or +1, it is not a reliable indicator of how similar a predictor is to random guessing because MCC is dependent on the dataset.[[10]](#cite_note-Chicco2021-10) MCC is closely related to the [chi-square statistic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pearson's_chi-square_test "Pearson's chi-square test") for a 2×2 [contingency table](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contingency_table "Contingency table")

:   ![{\displaystyle |{\text{MCC}}|={\sqrt {\frac {\chi ^{2}}{n}}}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/87f53eda55e29fc0a1506152051e0ff789c1708b)

where *n* is the total number of observations.

While there is no perfect way of describing the [confusion matrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confusion_matrix "Confusion matrix") of true and false positives and negatives by a single number, the Matthews correlation coefficient is generally regarded as being one of the best such measures.[[11]](#cite_note-Powers2011-11) Other measures, such as the proportion of correct predictions (also termed [accuracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accuracy "Accuracy")), are not useful when the two classes are of very different sizes. For example, assigning every object to the larger set achieves a high proportion of correct predictions, but is not generally a useful classification.

The MCC can be calculated directly from the [confusion matrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confusion_matrix "Confusion matrix") using the formula:

:   ![{\displaystyle {\text{MCC}}={\frac {{\mathit {TP}}\times {\mathit {TN}}-{\mathit {FP}}\times {\mathit {FN}}}{\sqrt {({\mathit {TP}}+{\mathit {FP}})({\mathit {TP}}+{\mathit {FN}})({\mathit {TN}}+{\mathit {FP}})({\mathit {TN}}+{\mathit {FN}})}}}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/33f3d62224f97cdef8bc559ee455c3f4815f5788)

In this equation, *TP* is the number of [true positives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/True_positive "True positive"), *TN* the number of [true negatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/True_negative "True negative"), *FP* the number of [false positives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/False_positive "False positi

The F-score is also used in machine learning. However, the F-measures do not take true negatives into account, hence measures such as the Matthews correlation coefficient, Informedness or Cohen's kappa may be preferred to assess the performance of a binary classifier.

The F-score has been widely used in the natural language processing literature, such as in the evaluation of named entity recognition and word segmentation.

## Properties

[edit] [...] David M W Powers") has pointed out that F1 ignores the True Negatives and thus is misleading for unbalanced classes, while kappa and correlation measures are symmetric and assess both directions of predictability - the classifier predicting the true class and the true class predicting the classifier prediction, proposing separate multiclass measures Informedness and Markedness for the two directions, noting that their geometric mean is correlation.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Statistical measure of a test's accuracy

For the significance test, see [F-test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F-test "F-test").

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/26/Precisionrecall.svg/500px-Precisionrecall.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Precisionrecall.svg)

Precision and recall

In [statistical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics "Statistics") analysis of [binary classification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_classification "Binary classification") and [information retrieval](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Information_retrieval "Information retrieval") systems, the **F-score** or **F-measure** is a measure of predictive performance. It is calculated from the [precision](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Precision_(information_retrieval) "Precision (information retrieval)") and [recall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recall_(information_retrieval) "Recall (information retrieval)") of the test, where the precision is the number of true positive results divided by the number of all samples predicted to be positive, including those not identified correctly, and the recall is the number of true positive results divided by the number of all samples that should have been identified as positive. Precision is also known as [positive predictive value](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Positive_predictive_value "Positive predictive value"), and recall is also known as [sensitivity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sensitivity_and_specificity "Sensitivity and specificity") in diagnostic binary classification.

The **F1** score is the [harmonic mean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmonic_mean "Harmonic mean") of the precision and recall. It thus symmetrically represents both precision and recall in one metric. The more generic ![{\displaystyle F_{\beta }}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/eb39f5958eb83bc3c28cd8b1a5397d3bb14fecdf) score applies additional weights, valuing one of precision or recall more than the other.

The highest possible value of an F-score is 1.0, indicating perfect precision and recall, and the lowest possible value is 0, if the precision or the recall is zero.

## Etymology

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=F-score&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Etymology")]

The name F-measure is believed to be named after a different F function in Van Rijsbergen's book, when introduced to the Fourth [Message Understanding Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Message_Understanding_Conference "Message Understanding Conference") (MUC-4, 1992).[[1]](#cite_note-1)

## Definition

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=F-score&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Definition")]

The traditional F-measure or balanced F-score (**F1 score**) is the [harmonic mean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmonic_mean#Harmonic_mean_of_two_numbers "Harmonic mean") of precision and recall:[[2]](#cite_note-2)

:   ![{\displaystyle F_{1}={\frac {2}{\mathrm {recall} ^{-1}+\mathrm {precision} ^{-1}}}=2{\frac {\mathrm {precision} \cdot \mathrm {recall} }{\mathrm {precision} +\mathrm {recall} }}={\frac {2\mathrm {TP} }{2\mathrm {TP} +\mathrm {FP} +\mathrm {FN} }}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/ee9b2235daf4402960538e73d6310bc8c2b8de52)

With precision = TP / (TP + FP) and recall = TP / (TP + FN), it follows that the numerator of *F*1 is the sum of their numerators and the denominator of *F*1 is the sum of their denominators.

If FP=FN

![{\displaystyle F_{1}={\frac {2\mathrm {TP} }{2\mathrm {TP} +2\mathrm {FP} }}={\frac {\mathrm {TP} }{\mathrm {TP} +\mathrm {FP} }}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/0cddca2607d87d90fa7a546e8258d80124c6a4d1)

or

![{\displaystyle F_{1}={\frac {2\mathrm {TP} }{2\mathrm {TP} +2\mathrm {FN} }}={\frac {\mathrm {TP} }{\mathrm {TP} +\mathrm {FN} }}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/71c0b4100c85bc8c99e4ed5d6c8dee136bf6befe)

So, F1 = precision = recall

If TP=FP=FN

![{\displaystyle F_{1}={\frac {2\mathrm {TP} }{2\mathrm {TP} +2\mathrm {FP} }}={\frac {2\mathrm {TP} }{4\mathrm {TP} }}={\frac {1}{2}}=0.5}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/99ebefa34cfcabd3b7c563404d666db1a6b70553)

or

![{\displaystyle F_{1}={\frac {2\mathrm {TP} }{2\mathrm {TP} +2\mathrm {FN} }}={\frac {2\mathrm {TP} }{4\mathrm {TP} }}={\frac {1}{2}}=0.5}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/656401fe1b3f9c3c054a3ce724d0685d09899870)

To see it as a harmonic mean, note that ![{\displaystyle F_{1}^{-1}={\frac {1}{2}}(\mathrm {recall} ^{-1}+\mathrm {precision} ^{-1})}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/31417c2f9121c58b8729ffbef6434aa1c659d61c).

### Fβ score

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=F-score&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Fβ score")]

A more general F score, ![{\displaystyle F_{\beta }}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/eb39f5958eb83bc3c28cd8b1a5397d3bb14fecdf), that uses a positive real factor ![{\displaystyle \beta }](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/7ed48a5e36207156fb792fa79d29925d2f7901e8), where ![{\displaystyle \beta }](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/7ed48a5e36207156fb792fa79d29925d2f7901e8) is chosen such that recall is considered ![{\displaystyle \beta ^{2}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/1a79f17c76984dead8b0c072b4fdf537b13895e7) times as important as precision, is:

:   ![{\displaystyle F_{\beta }={\frac {\beta ^{2}+1}{(\beta ^{2}\cdot \mathrm {recall} ^{-1})+\mathrm {precision} ^{-1}}}={\frac {(1+\beta ^{2})\cdot \mathrm {precision} \cdot \mathrm {recall} }{(\beta ^{2}\cdot \mathrm {precision} )+\mathrm {recall} }}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/052f8aedae417f7e6a65efe8b72576aa7cbb2d60)

To see that as a weighted harmonic mean, note that ![{\displaystyle F_{\beta }^{-1}={\frac {1}{\beta +\beta ^{-1}}}(\beta \cdot \mathrm {recall} ^{-1}+\beta ^{-1}\cdot \mathrm {precision} ^{-1})}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/8ee5319fb06760a1611defb4197dfdd000a87ae9).

In terms of [Type I and type II errors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Type_I_and_type_II_errors "Type I and type II errors") this becomes:

:   ![{\displaystyle F_{\beta }={\frac {(1+\beta ^{2})\cdot \mathrm {TP} }{(1+\beta ^{2})\cdot \mathrm {TP} +\beta ^{2}\cdot \mathrm {FN} +\mathrm {FP} }}\,={\frac {(1+\beta ^{2})\cdot \mathrm {TP} }{(\mathrm {TP} +\mathrm {FN} )\cdot \beta ^{2}+(\mathrm {TP} +\mathrm {FP} )}}\,}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/b4e6bf3291ff14fc89b2fa7dc00589e59e216224)

Two commonly used values for ![{\displaystyle \beta }](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/7ed48a5e36207156fb792fa79d29925d2f7901e8) are 2, which weighs recall higher than precision, and 1/2, which weighs recall lower than precision.

The F-measure was derived so that ![{\displaystyle F_{\beta }}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/eb39f5958eb83bc3c28cd8b1a5397d3bb14fecdf) "measures the effectiveness of retrieval with respect to a user who attaches ![{\displaystyle \beta }](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/7ed48a5e36207156fb792fa79d29925d2f7901e8) times as much importance to recall as precision".[[3]](#cite_note-3) It is based on [Van Rijsbergen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C._J._van_Rijsbergen "C. J. van Rijsbergen")'s effectiveness measure

:   ![{\displaystyle E=1-\left({\frac {\alpha }{p}}+{\frac {1-\alpha }{r}}\right)^{-1}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/fbf2de0adedf04b55032e75ccc9a09cb39ab7bd9)

Their relationship is: ![{\displaystyle F_{\beta }=1-E}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/588a56674a39e59ba281d71e792a2a702326ecec) where ![{\displaystyle \alpha ={\frac {1}{1+\beta ^{2}}}}](https

In [statistics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics "Statistics"), **inter-rater reliability** (also called by various similar names, such as **inter-rater agreement**, **inter-rater concordance**, **inter-observer reliability**, **inter-coder reliability**, and so on) is the degree of agreement among independent observers who rate, code, or assess the same phenomenon.

Assessment tools that rely on ratings must exhibit good inter-rater reliability, otherwise they are not [valid tests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Test_validity "Test validity").

There are a number of statistics that can be used to determine inter-rater reliability. Different statistics are appropriate for different types of measurement. Some options are joint-probability of agreement, such as [Cohen's kappa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cohen's_kappa "Cohen's kappa"), [Scott's pi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott's_pi "Scott's pi") and [Fleiss' kappa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fleiss'_kappa "Fleiss' kappa"); or inter-rater correlation, [concordance correlation coefficient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concordance_correlation_coefficient "Concordance correlation coefficient"), [intra-class correlation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intra-class_correlation "Intra-class correlation"), and [Krippendorff's alpha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krippendorff's_alpha "Krippendorff's alpha").

## Concept

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Inter-rater_reliability&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Concept")]

There are several operational definitions of "inter-rater reliability," reflecting different viewpoints about what is a reliable agreement between raters.[[1]](#cite_note-1) There are three operational definitions of agreement:

1. Reliable raters agree with the "official" rating of a performance.
2. Reliable raters agree with each other about the exact ratings to be awarded.
3. Reliable raters agree about which performance is better and which is worse.

These combine with two operational definitions of behavior:

1. Reliable raters are automatons, behaving like "rating machines". This category includes rating of essays by computer[[2]](#cite_note-2) This behavior can be evaluated by [generalizability theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generalizability_theory "Generalizability theory").
2. Reliable raters behave like independent witnesses. They demonstrate their independence by disagreeing slightly. This behavior can be evaluated by the [Rasch model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rasch_model "Rasch model").

## Statistics

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Inter-rater_reliability&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Statistics")]

### Joint probability of agreement

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Inter-rater_reliability&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Joint probability of agreement")]

The joint-probability of agreement is the simplest and the least robust measure. It is estimated as the percentage of the time the raters agree in a [nominal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nominal_data "Nominal data") or categorical rating system. It does not take into account the fact that agreement may happen solely based on chance. There is some question whether or not there is a need to 'correct' for chance agreement; some suggest that, in any case, any such adjustment should be based on an explicit model of how chance and error affect raters' decisions.[[3]](#cite_note-3)

When the number of categories being used is small (e.g. 2 or 3), the likelihood for 2 raters to agree by pure chance increases dramatically. This is because both raters must confine themselves to the limited number of options available, which impacts the overall agreement rate, and not necessarily their propensity for "intrinsic" agreement (an agreement is considered "intrinsic" if it is not due to chance).

Therefore, the joint probability of agreement will remain high even in the absence of any "intrinsic" agreement among raters. A useful inter-rater reliability coefficient is expected (a) to be close to 0 when there is no "intrinsic" agreement and (b) to increase as the "intrinsic" agreement rate improves. Most chance-corrected agreement coefficients achieve the first objective. However, the second objective is not achieved by many known chance-corrected measures.[[4]](#cite_note-4)

### Kappa statistics

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Inter-rater_reliability&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Kappa statistics")]

Main articles: [Cohen's kappa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cohen's_kappa "Cohen's kappa") and [Fleiss' kappa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fleiss'_kappa "Fleiss' kappa")

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fd/Comparison_of_rubrics_for_evaluating_inter-rater_kappa_%28and_intra-class_correlation%29_coefficients.png/250px-Comparison_of_rubrics_for_evaluating_inter-rater_kappa_%28and_intra-class_correlation%29_coefficients.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Comparison_of_rubrics_for_evaluating_inter-rater_kappa_(and_intra-class_correlation)_coefficients.png)

Four sets of recommendations for interpreting level of inter-rater agreement

Kappa is a way of measuring agreement or reliability, correcting for how often ratings might agree by chance. Cohen's kappa,[[5]](#cite_note-5) which works for two raters, and Fleiss' kappa,[[6]](#cite_note-6) an adaptation that works for any fixed number of raters, improve upon the joint probability in that they take into account the amount of agreement that could be expected to occur through chance. The original versions had the same problem as [the joint-probability](#Joint_probability_of_agreement) in that they treat the data as nominal and assume the ratings have no natural ordering; if the data actually have a rank (ordinal level of measurement), then that information is not fully considered in the measurements.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Descriptive statistic

In [statistics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics "Statistics"), the **intraclass correlation**, or the **intraclass correlation coefficient** (**ICC**),[[1]](#cite_note-1) is a [descriptive statistic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Descriptive_statistic "Descriptive statistic") that can be used when quantitative measurements are made on units that are organized into groups. It describes how strongly units in the same group resemble each other. While it is viewed as a type of [correlation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Correlation "Correlation"), unlike most other correlation measures, it operates on data structured as groups rather than data structured as paired observations.

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f2/ICC-example2.svg/330px-ICC-example2.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:ICC-example2.svg)

A [dot plot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dot_plot_(statistics) "Dot plot (statistics)") showing a data set with high intraclass correlation. Values from the same group tend to be similar.

 [![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c9/ICC-example1.svg/330px-ICC-example1.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:ICC-example1.svg)

A [dot plot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dot_plot_(statistics) "Dot plot (statistics)") showing a data set with low intraclass correlation. There is very little tendency for values from the same group to be similar.

The *intraclass correlation* is commonly used to quantify the degree to which individuals with a fixed degree of relatedness (e.g. full siblings) resemble each other in terms of a quantitative trait (see [heritability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heritability "Heritability")). Another prominent application is the assessment of consistency or reproducibility of quantitative measurements made by different observers measuring the same quantity.

## Early ICC definition: unbiased but complex formula

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Intraclass_correlation&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early ICC definition: unbiased but complex formula")]

The earliest work on intraclass correlations focused on the case of paired measurements, and the first intraclass correlation (ICC) statistics to be proposed were modifications of the [interclass correlation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pearson_product_moment_correlation_coefficient "Pearson product moment correlation coefficient") (Pearson correlation).

Consider a [data set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_set "Data set") consisting of *N* [paired data](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paired_data "Paired data") values (*x**n*,1, *x**n*,2), for *n* = 1, ..., *N*. The intraclass correlation *r* originally proposed[[2]](#cite_note-2) by [Ronald Fisher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Fisher "Ronald Fisher")[[3]](#cite_note-FisherR1954Statistical-3) is

:   ![{\displaystyle r={\frac {1}{Ns^{2}}}\sum _{n=1}^{N}(x_{n,1}-{\bar {x}})(x_{n,2}-{\bar {x}}),}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/5837b5a4ef51ad2442cecf4d320e68d8b1fd3450)

where

:   ![{\displaystyle {\bar {x}}={\frac {1}{2N}}\sum _{n=1}^{N}(x_{n,1}+x_{n,2}),}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/212c60e2a07cab4daebe30f5be157128132e04c0)
:   ![{\displaystyle s^{2}={\frac {1}{2N}}\left\{\sum _{n=1}^{N}(x_{n,1}-{\bar {x}})^{2}+\sum _{n=1}^{N}(x_{n,2}-{\bar {x}})^{2}\right\}.}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/63c1e81038cebc882fb5fc0dba93f5f89c1957d6)

Later versions of this statistic [[3]](#cite_note-FisherR1954Statistical-3) used the [degrees of freedom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Degrees_of_freedom_(statistics) "Degrees of freedom (statistics)") 2*N* −1 in the denominator for calculating *s*2 and *N* −1 in the denominator for calculating *r*, so that *s*2 becomes unbiased, and *r* becomes unbiased if *s* is known.

The key difference between this ICC and the [interclass (Pearson) correlation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pearson_product-moment_correlation_coefficient "Pearson product-moment correlation coefficient") is that the data are pooled to estimate the mean and variance. The reason for this is that in the setting where an intraclass correlation is desired, the pairs are considered to be unordered. For example, if we are studying the resemblance of twins, there is usually no meaningful way to order the values for the two individuals within a twin pair. Like the interclass correlation, the intraclass correlation for paired data will be confined to the [interval](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interval_(mathematics) "Interval (mathematics)") [−1, +1].

The intraclass correlation is also defined for data sets with groups having more than 2 values. For groups consisting of three values, it is defined as[[3]](#cite_note-FisherR1954Statistical-3)

:   ![{\displaystyle r={\frac {1}{3Ns^{2}}}\sum _{n=1}^{N}\left\{(x_{n,1}-{\bar {x}})(x_{n,2}-{\bar {x}})+(x_{n,1}-{\bar {x}})(x_{n,3}-{\bar {x}})+(x_{n,2}-{\bar {x}})(x_{n,3}-{\bar {x}})\right\},}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/210c531e888c084220bcfff8a78ee17d60405ae2)

where

:   ![{\displaystyle {\bar {x}}={\frac {1}{3N}}\sum _{n=1}^{N}(x_{n,1}+x_{n,2}+x_{n,3}),}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/28a0a66e8b23ca0e8ccc5d825ab33c21305698e2)
:   ![{\displaystyle s^{2}={\frac {1}{3N}}\left\{\sum _{n=1}^{N}(x_{n,1}-{\bar {x}})^{2}+\sum _{n=1}^{N}(x_{n,2}-{\bar {x}})^{2}+\sum _{n=1}^{N}(x_{n,3}-{\bar {x}})^{2}\right\}.}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/bc2c81f349abbef7b940e9554635983f5032dcc9)

As the number of items per group grows, so does the number of cross-product terms in this expression grows. The following equivalent form is simpler to calculate:

:   ![{\displaystyle r={\frac {K}{K-1}}\cdot {\frac {N^{-1}\sum _{n=1}^{N}({\bar {x}}_{n}-{\bar {x}})^{2}}{s^{2}}}-{\frac {1}{K-1}},}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/708a3b585fa1bf7d8b930007046106547e4c3fbd)

where *K* is the number of data values per group, and ![{\displaystyle {\bar {x}}_{n}}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/0228b0d7b888e15823ac37c461bd4b220151512a) is the sample mean of the *n*th group.[[3]](#cite_note-FisherR1954Statistical-3) This form is usually attributed to [Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Arthur_Harris "James Arthur Harris").[[4]](#cite_note-4) The left term is non-negative; consequently the intraclass correlation must satisfy

:   ![{\displaystyle r\geq {\frac {-1}{K-1}}.}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/0c311ffdb9c8a4257ef36d6ae97bd4178a2aa6b8)

For large *K*, this ICC is nearly equal to

:   ![{\displaystyle {\frac {N^{-1}\sum _{n=1}^{N}({\bar {x}}_{n}-{\bar {x}})^{2}}{s^{2}}},}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/324f2f784757628d0ecab56a1798105ba173563d)

which can be interpreted as the fraction of the total variance that is due to variation between groups. [Ronald Fisher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Fisher "Ronald Fisher") devotes an entire chapter to intraclass correlation in his classic book *[Statistical Methods for Research Workers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistical_Methods_for_Research_Workers "Statistical Methods for Research Workers")*.[[3]](#cite_note-FisherR1954Statistical-3)

For data from a population that is completely noise, Fisher's formula produces ICC values that are distributed about 0, i.e. sometimes being negative. This is because Fisher designed the formula to be unbiased, and therefore its estimates are sometimes overestimates and sometimes underestimates. For small or 0 underlying values in the population, the ICC calculated from a sample may be negative.

## Modern ICC definitions: simpler formula but positive bias

[[edit](/w/index
